clue.text: Wood in the role of fence

blocks.note: 'as' means in the role of, as in 'acting as'
a pen is an enclosure, a fence round animals

explanation.surface: Timber being used as a fence around a field.
explanation.definitionFit: The aspen is a poplar tree, and its timber or a stand of such trees counts as wood.

clue.text: Topless dance with vermin stopped by teacher, hairy thing

indicators.note: without a top, so the dance loses its first letter
a word stopped by another has that other plugged into its middle

blocks.note: the tango is a ballroom dance
the rat is classic vermin
a rabbi is a Jewish teacher of the law

explanation.surface: A list of oddities: a dance done topless, rats interrupted by a teacher, some hairy creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hairy thing' sounds dismissive, but it is a fair description of a pet bred for its long fleece; 'topless' takes only the first letter off.
explanation.definitionFit: This breed of domestic rabbit is famous for its long, silky coat, used for wool, so it is very much a furry creature.

clue.text: Priest legendary Christian John has held close

indicators.note: the legendary figure has something held inside his name

blocks.note: Prester John was a mythical Christian king of the East in medieval legend
'close by' means near, so by = close

explanation.surface: A legendary figure keeping a priest close at hand.
explanation.walkthrough: Prester John is the medieval legend of a Christian priest-king; split his first name around BY.
explanation.definitionFit: A presbyter is an elder or priest in the early Church and in Presbyterian churches, a synonym for priest.

clue.text: Rump chewed in Cockney mouth?

indicators.note: the eating goes inside the mouth, between its two ends

blocks.note: in rhyming slang mouth is 'north and south', and north and south are N and S
chewed means ate

explanation.surface: Someone chewing rump steak with a London accent.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney rhyming slang swaps a word for a rhyming phrase: mouth is 'north and south', which the setter boils down to the compass letters N and S.
explanation.definitionFit: Nates is the anatomical Latin plural for the buttocks, which together make up the rump of a body.

clue.text: Breezy isle, 'aughty

blocks.note: Unst is the most northerly inhabited island of Shetland
haughty is huffy; the apostrophe dropping the H of 'aughty tells you to drop the H of huffy too

explanation.surface: A windswept island with a snooty, h-dropping local.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe is the device: 'aughty is haughty with its H lost, so its synonym huffy loses its H as well.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone unstuffy is relaxed and informal, which matches the casual, carefree sense of breezy.

clue.text: Looking north, infernal (?) gala regularly seen, fire festival

indicators.note: regularly means taking every other letter at even intervals

blocks.note: in a down clue, looking north means up
a jokey adjective from hell, hence the query
the second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: A northern, devilishly hot gala famous for its bonfire.
explanation.walkthrough: Up Helly Aa is held every January in Lerwick, Shetland, where a replica Viking longship is burnt.
explanation.definitionFit: This Shetland celebration ends with torch-bearers setting a Viking galley ablaze, so it is literally a festival of fire.

clue.text: Something of a 8 24, tissue that's bagged

indicators.note: letters bagged by the phrase are held within it

blocks.note: found across the two words

explanation.surface: A haggis ingredient: tissue stuffed into a bag.
explanation.walkthrough: 8 24 is the Burns phrase for a haggis, a pudding of offal, oatmeal and fat cooked in a sheep's stomach.
explanation.definitionFit: Suet, the hard fat from around kidneys, is a standard ingredient of haggis, so it is part of one.

clue.text: Yet to be entertained by working of nut?

blocks.note: the surface: an idea nobody has yet considered
the setter's reading: the nut is the head, and its working is thinking, so this is something the head has not processed; the word also opens with a jumble of the letters of nut

explanation.walkthrough: 'Nut' is slang for the head, so the working of the nut is thought; an idea not yet entertained has not been through that process.
explanation.definitionFit: To entertain an idea is to consider it, so an idea yet to be entertained has never been thought of.

clue.text: See 21 Across
17s' titan, other than that pure grace, deified icon

indicators.note: the words that follow are to be made other, into a different form

blocks.clueFragment: than that pure grace, deified icon
blocks.note: twenty-eight letters, every one used

explanation.surface: Praise for a hero of Burns, mightier than any pure, god-like icon.
explanation.walkthrough: 17 is BURNS, the poet. 'Other than' looks like a phrase meaning except; only 'other' is the signal. The words are a line from his poem Address to a Haggis.
explanation.definitionFit: Burns hails the haggis as the great chieftain of the pudding-race, so this title is the poet's giant of puddings.

clue.text: One's in Gaia, then another – and in another also!

definitions.text: One's in Gaia, then another – and in another also!

blocks.note: the surface: Gaia herself is one such deity

blocks.clueFragment: then another – and in another also
blocks.note: the setter's reading: 'Gaia then another' hides Athena, and 'another also' hides Hera, two more of the same kind

explanation.walkthrough: Gaia is the earth mother of Greek myth; the run 'gaiA THEN Another' holds Athena and 'anotHER Also' holds Hera.
explanation.definitionFit: Gaia, Athena and Hera are all female deities of the Olympian mythology of ancient Greece.

clue.text: In solid style, work of art in fat, not half!

indicators.note: only one half of the doubled word for fat is kept
the art goes inside the word for fat

blocks.note: a bust is a sculpture of head and shoulders
roly-poly means plump

explanation.surface: A sturdy sculpture placed among fat, with a mocking 'not half!'
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half!' sounds like British slang for 'very much', but it means halving roly-poly to ROLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something robustly means doing it in a sturdy, strong manner, which is a solid style.

clue.text: Regular on shipping forecast – might one follow?

blocks.note: first meaning: a sea area in the North Sea named on the BBC shipping forecast
second meaning: one who dogs, trailing someone

explanation.walkthrough: The shipping forecast is a BBC radio bulletin reading out weather for named sea areas round Britain; Dogger comes up every time.
explanation.definitionFit: Dogger is a named North Sea area always read out, and to dog is to follow, so a dogger tails someone.

clue.text: One charged for utilities per year, with tax cut for building

indicators.note: the levy is cut short, losing its last letter
the letters are raw material to build something new from

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A bill for gas and water per year, plus a reduced tax on a building.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Per year' looks like part of the definition but is the fodder. Rates were the British local property tax paid by householders.
explanation.definitionFit: A ratepayer paid the local rates that funded council services such as water and drains, so is someone billed for them.

clue.text: Deadly when confined, steps taken to break in

indicators.note: something that breaks in forces its way inside the other word

blocks.note: pent, as in pent up, means shut in
a stile is a set of steps for climbing over a fence

explanation.surface: A deadly lock-up broken into by burglars using steps.
explanation.definitionFit: Pestilent describes something that spreads fatal disease like a plague, so it is lethal.

clue.text: In plaster, yours truly is up for rest

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading from bottom to top
the phrase goes inside the word for plaster

blocks.note: render is a coat of plaster on a wall
yours truly is me, so the phrase becomes 'I am'

explanation.surface: The writer is stuck in a plaster cast, laid up to rest.
explanation.walkthrough: Yours truly is the writer's way of saying me, so 'yours truly is' turns into I AM.
explanation.definitionFit: The rest of something is what is left over, which is the meaning of remainder.

clue.text: Wind into which leading character in blockbuster has gone – him?

indicators.note: the leading character of a word is its first letter
something goes into the wind word, which then holds it
having gone into the wind word, the letter now sits inside it

blocks.note: a gale is a strong wind
the first letter

explanation.surface: Wind, blockbuster, has gone: read together, Gone with the Wind, so 'him?' asks who starred.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue's words spell out the 1939 film Gone with the Wind; 'him' is its leading man Clark Gable.
explanation.definitionFit: Clark Gable played Rhett Butler, the male star of the epic film Gone with the Wind.

clue.text: Poisonous agent in business maintaining a house standing on a road

indicators.note: in a down clue, standing up means read from bottom to top
to maintain is to hold, so the business word holds the next piece

blocks.note: biz is informal for business, as in showbiz
A plus HO, the abbreviation for house
A plus RD, the abbreviation for road

explanation.surface: A firm storing a toxin in a house beside a road.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts one piece below another, so A RD comes after the rest.
explanation.definitionFit: A biohazard is a biological substance, such as a toxin or germ, that endangers health, so a harmful agent.

clue.text: Flower of Scotland's poet

blocks.note: a flower is something that flows, and a Scottish stream is a burn
taken as written

explanation.surface: Flower of Scotland is the Scottish anthem; here it seems to belong to a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is crossword code for a river, something that flows, and the Scots word for a stream is burn.
explanation.definitionFit: Robert Burns, Scotland's national bard, is the most famous Scottish poet.

clue.text: Moonwalker able to pack a punch?

blocks.note: first meaning: Neil, the first man on the Moon
second meaning, split in two: having a strong arm

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the second reading as a pun: the name broken up describes someone with a strong arm.
explanation.definitionFit: Neil Armstrong walked on the Moon in 1969, and someone arm-strong has the muscle to hit hard.

clue.text: Nordic girl appearing as an answer?

blocks.note: first meaning: a Scandinavian woman's name
second meaning, split in two: written into the crossword's squares

explanation.walkthrough: The question mark warns that the second definition is a pun: a solved answer is in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: Ingrid is a common Scandinavian female name, as with Ingrid Bergman, and an answer sits in the grid.

clue.text: Try time and time again, a must

blocks.note: to have a go is to try
T is the abbreviation for time, here used twice
taken as written

explanation.surface: Persevering again and again because success is a must.
explanation.definitionFit: Gotta is the informal contraction of 'have got to', meaning one is obliged, as in 'I gotta go'.

clue.text: Some tripping up, settle affair

blocks.note: up means high
to land is to settle, as a bird does
a fling is a brief love affair

explanation.surface: Someone on a drug trip, high, settling a love affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tripping up' looks like stumbling, but 'tripping' alone is the dancing, as in 'trip the light fantastic', and 'up' starts the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A highland fling is a lively Scottish solo dance, so it is an instance of light-footed dancing.

clue.text: Feeling bump

blocks.note: first meaning: an intuition
second meaning: a hump, as on a hunchback

explanation.definitionFit: A hunch is a gut intuition about something, and also a lump or protuberance on the back.

clue.text: Isle manure

blocks.note: first meaning: a small island of the Inner Hebrides off western Scotland
second meaning: dung, farmyard filth

explanation.definitionFit: Muck is one of the Small Isles south of Skye, and the word also means dung spread on fields.

clue.text: See 8
Leave debauched rake, drinker say?

indicators.note: debauched means corrupted, so the letters are perverted into a new order

blocks.note: to part is to leave
the four letters of the word rake

explanation.surface: A debauched rake, a heavy drinker, being told to leave.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Debauched rake' paints a libertine, which makes 'drinker' look like a description of him.
explanation.definitionFit: To partake is to consume food or drink, so a drinker is one example of a partaker, hence 'say?'.

clue.text: God in beachwear, but no cap

indicators.note: without its cap means the top, or first, letter goes

blocks.note: shades are sunglasses worn on the beach

explanation.surface: A deity on the beach in swimwear but without a hat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No cap' looks like a bare head on the beach, but the cap is the first letter of the beachwear.
explanation.definitionFit: Hades is the Greek god of the underworld, brother of Zeus and Poseidon.
